title: Epoch budget also clears the noise floor: 8 -> 24 epochs is +0.0068 on small
description: CONFIRMED, final: 24-epoch small 0.8205 vs 8-epoch 0.8081 = +0.0124, twice the noise floor. Curve peaked around epoch 18-21 then flattened (0.8187-0.8189 at 22-23), so ~20-24 epochs is roughly the right budget for small at this data size. Larger than the encoder change (+0.0085), and a 24-epoch SMALL model beats an 8-epoch BASE one (0.8166). CONSEQUENCE: every arm in the ablation ledger was run at 8 epochs against a baseline that had not converged, so 'no measured effect' there means 'measured in the wrong regime'. The five leaderboard members are 8-epoch; retraining the same recipe at ~24 is worth about +0.012 before anything else changes.

title: DINOv2-base clears the noise floor: +0.0085, needs seeds and more epochs
description: COMPOSES with the epoch budget. Matched fold-0 ladder on report_labels_v2: small 8ep 0.8081, base 8ep 0.8166 (+0.0085), small 24ep 0.8205 (+0.0124), base 20ep 0.8242 at epoch 14 of 20 (+0.0161, ~2.6x the 0.0062 floor). The two capacity levers add rather than substitute. Submission recipe is therefore base + 20 epochs + batch 12; a 5-fold retrain is queued (about 93 minutes) and the base submission path is already dry-run verified on the host (variant resolves, mount matches, fingerprint check passes).

title: Per-slice encoding with max pooling, and a CNN backbone — the only untested difference of the right size
description:
EVERY KNOB IS EXHAUSTED AND THEY ARE ALL THE SAME SIZE. Measured on this architecture: schedule +0.0061, augmentation-applied +0.0110, TTA +0.0035, intensity augmentation +0.0019, weight floor +0.0019, better labels -0.0008, 32 slices -0.018. Apart from the three defects, nothing is worth more than 0.002.

THE REMAINING GAPS ARE AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE BIGGER: our per-member holdout 0.8269 against the .903 reference's reported OOF 0.8544, and 0.888 against the leader's 0.942. Nothing measured explains either.

THE .903 RECIPE DIFFERS STRUCTURALLY, NOT BY SETTINGS:
  backbone     single-channel ImageNet EfficientNet-B3   (ours: DINOv2-small ViT, 3-channel)
  study input  3 fluid-sensitive plane-diverse series    (ours: 6 plane x weighting slots)
  pooling      MAX over slice embeddings, then MEAN over series logits
               (ours: 3 consecutive slices stacked as CHANNELS, then per-diagnosis attention over slots)

THE POOLING DIFFERENCE IS THE ONE WITH A MECHANISM WE HAVE ALREADY FELT. Our channel stacking is what made 32 inference slices FAIL (-0.018): raising the slice count over a fixed band changes each group's physical thickness, so the model sees an input distribution it never trained on. Per-slice encoding has no such coupling — which is exactly why THEY can raise slices at inference and we cannot. The same coupling plausibly limits what a fixed 12-slice budget can see: a finding is either inside a sampled 3-slice group or invisible.

WHY IT IS NOW AFFORDABLE: `StudyModel` already takes its backbone as an injected `nn.Module` (structural, not a named protocol — written that way for exactly this), and timm 1.0.26 is in Kaggle's image, so an EfficientNet needs no wheel. What has to change is the bag layout and `_pool`.

SCOPE, and it is genuinely two experiments that should not be confused:
  1. AGGREGATION: keep DINOv2, encode each slice independently, max over slices. Isolates pooling.
  2. BACKBONE: keep the aggregation, swap the encoder. Isolates the encoder family.
Run 1 first — it is the one with a mechanism we have already observed, and it does not need a new model mount.

CAVEAT THAT MUST NOT BE FORGOTTEN: at ~0.002 per knob and an unmeasured noise floor, a single fold cannot resolve a small win here either. This is worth doing only because the hypothesised effect is 0.02-0.03, not 0.002 — if it lands in the noise, it is a refutation, not a tuning opportunity.
close_reason: REFUTED at the predicted size: per-slice max +0.0018 vs 0.0012 noise floor, for 3x encoder cost, on a matched pair (0.8099 vs 0.8081). The mechanism was also wrong - 32-slice inference costs the same -0.01 under BOTH poolings, so channel-stacking's thickness coupling was not why the wide read hurt. Backbone swap (experiment 2) not run: experiment 1 was the one with an observed mechanism and it did not survive.

title: We train on the second-worst public label table; a better one is free
description:
MEASURED ON THE 58 GOLD STUDIES (2026-08-11), mean per-finding AUC of each public reader against the expert annotations:

  pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels      0.8705   <- WHAT WE TRAIN ON
  stevenleehans llm_labels_v2        0.8905
  stevenleehans llm_labels_v4_blend  0.8982   <- +0.028, free, already public
  lixin73 report_labels_gpt56sol     0.8431

Per finding the gaps are much larger than the mean suggests: Synovitis 0.695 (pilkwang) against 0.805, Contusion 0.756 against 0.862, Lateral Meniscus 0.844 against 0.886. Those are three of our four weakest labels on the holdout, and each costs a full 1/12 of the competition metric.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE NUMBER: the .903 notebook states plainly that 'the image model is downstream of label quality'. We have been tuning the model (schedule, augmentation, TTA) against labels that are 0.028 worse than the best freely available ones, so every one of those measurements was made against a handicapped target.

FUSION IS REFUTED FOR OUR READERS, which is worth recording because the .903 system's headline mechanism is fusion:
  mean of all four        0.8938
  rank-mean of all four   0.8966
  rank-mean of top three  0.8952
  best single (steven_v4) 0.8982   <- still the winner
Averaging drags the best table toward the weaker ones, and v4_blend is ALREADY a blend, so there is little independent signal left to add. Their fusion presumably worked because their private Qwen reader was independent of pilkwang's; ours are not.

DO NOT hand-pick a per-finding winner. The oracle that does scores 0.9016, but it is chosen on the same 57 studies it is scored on, and at these counts a per-finding AUC carries roughly +/-0.09. That is the same trap the annotation check sets (identical members scoring 0.7356 to 0.9164 on it).

ACTION: retrain on steven_v4_blend and re-measure. Every recipe result so far (schedule +0.0061, augmentation +0.011) should be re-confirmed against the better labels, because a gain measured against noisier targets can shrink or grow when the targets improve.
notes:
SWAP NEEDS NO CODE (2026-08-11). `Targets.load` already handles the better table unchanged:

  report_labels_v2 (ours)   7 distinct target values, 12 __conf columns, mean weight 0.692
  llm_labels_v4_blend       186 distinct target values, NO __conf columns, mean weight 1.026

The absence of __conf is not a gap to fill. pilkwang's table carries a coarse score (five levels) plus a separate confidence; v4_blend carries a genuinely continuous score, so the uncertainty lives IN the target rather than beside it. BCE against 0.5 already pulls weakly in both directions, so adding a derived confidence would double-count the same doubt. It is also exactly what the .903 recipe does: 'BCE-with-logits on fused soft labels'.

CONSEQUENCE FOR AN OPEN ISSUE: with uniform weights, knee-9sy (the 0.25 weight floor) becomes moot under these labels — a floor only matters when some weights are zero, and none are. It stays open only for the old table.

QUEUED, so the GPU never idles between the five-fold run finishing and the ablations starting:
  A  fold 0, v4_blend labels, otherwise the recipe that scored 0.8202  -> isolates LABELS
  B  fold 0, v4_blend + intensity augmentation                        -> both changes together
  C  fold 0, old labels + intensity augmentation                      -> isolates AUGMENTATION

A, B and C against the 0.8202 baseline give both main effects and the interaction from three runs rather than four, because the baseline already exists.
METHODOLOGY BUG IN MY OWN ABLATION, caught mid-flight (2026-08-11).

`train.py` used ONE label table for both training and scoring, so the queued arms would have been measured with different rulers: the 0.8202 baseline was scored against pilkwang targets, while arm A (trained on v4_blend) would have been scored against v4_blend targets. A holdout AUC can rise simply because the labels agree with THEMSELVES more, and I would have read that as a better model.

FIX: `--eval-labels` separates the ruler from the training signal, defaulting to `--labels` so existing behaviour is unchanged.

RULER CHOSEN DELIBERATELY: pilkwang for every arm — the table the baseline used, and NOT the table the interesting arm trains on. A v4-trained model therefore earns no self-agreement credit; it is judged by the other reader. That makes the test conservative: it can understate v4's benefit but cannot manufacture one. If training on v4 improves a pilkwang-scored holdout, the labels are genuinely better rather than merely more self-consistent.

ARMS (fold 0, all scored on pilkwang):
  baseline  train pilkwang               0.8202  (already measured)
  A         train v4_blend               -> LABELS, conservative
  C         train pilkwang + intensity   -> AUGMENTATION, clean
  B         train v4_blend + intensity   -> both

45 minutes of GPU were killed to fix this rather than spending them on numbers that could not be compared.
ARM A RESULT — BETTER LABELS ARE NEUTRAL HERE (2026-08-11), which does not support the thesis I filed this issue on.

  baseline  train pilkwang, eval pilkwang   0.8202
  A         train v4_blend, eval pilkwang   0.8194   (-0.0008, i.e. flat)

The label tables differ by +0.028 in agreement with the 58 gold studies, and that difference did NOT translate into a better model on this measurement.

WHAT THE RESULT DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH, since the ruler is not neutral:
- The ruler is pilkwang, so the BASELINE enjoys a self-agreement advantage that arm A does not. 'Flat on a ruler tilted toward the baseline' is therefore weak evidence that v4 is at least as good, and is NOT evidence that it is worse.
- Equally, it is not the win the label-quality measurement suggested. BCE against soft targets is fairly robust to label noise, and both tables are derived from the SAME reports by different readers — so the readers' disagreement may be concentrated on studies whose reports are genuinely ambiguous, where neither label is reliable and the image cannot settle it either.

THE TEST THAT WOULD SETTLE IT is a cross-fitted evaluation on the 58 gold studies: each gold study scored only by the fold-model that held it out, for both label choices. Fold 0's holdout contains roughly a dozen gold studies, far too few alone, so this needs all five folds per arm — about 2.5 hours of GPU. That is the honest price of an unbiased ruler, and it is worth paying only if the augmentation arm does not turn out to be the larger lever.

DO NOT quietly switch the training labels on the strength of a label-quality number. The measurement that matters is the model's, and it says nothing so far.
CORRECTION (2026-08-11): closed as 'null' on a single-fold matched pair, but seed variance on the same fold is +/-0.012 while these effects are +/-0.002. The correct verdict is NOT DETECTABLE at n=1, not null. Neither is worth re-running bigger — resolving 0.002 against 0.012 needs ~36 paired runs — but the record should not claim more than it measured. See knee-uxg.
close_reason: Null on the model's own measurement (-0.0013 mean) despite +0.028 label quality against gold. Do not switch training labels on a label-quality number alone.

title: Augmentation was written, tested, and never called by the training loop
description:
FOUND 2026-08-11. `Trainer.augment` exists, is unit-tested, and `fit_epoch` NEVER CALLED IT. Every run to this point — all five folds and BOTH leaderboard submissions — trained with zero augmentation.

EVIDENCE IT MATTERED: the 40-epoch OneCycle curve peaks near epoch 16 and then declines monotonically (0.8143 -> 0.8043 by ep36). That is textbook overfitting, and it explains how they train 60 epochs where we degrade after 16.

WHY BOTH GATES MISSED IT, which is the part worth keeping:
- vulture (dead code) saw the method as USED, because its unit test references it.
- the mirror gate saw it as TESTED, because it has a `test_augment`.
A method can therefore be fully covered and completely disconnected. The gates check that a method exists, is referenced and is tested; none of them checks that the CALLER calls it.

FIX: `fit_epoch` now routes every batch through `augment_bag`, which converts uint8 -> float, warps, and converts back so `StudyModel.forward` (and therefore the fingerprint) is untouched. Slots are warped independently: they are separate acquisitions of one knee, not one volume, so a shared jitter would imply a registration that does not exist.

NEW TEST that would have caught it: `test_fit_epoch_augments` wraps `augment_bag` and asserts the training loop actually calls it. The general lesson: test the CALLER, not only the callee.
notes:
FIXED AND MEASURED (2026-08-11). Fold 0, every run matched on seed and data, only the recipe differing:

  constant LR, no aug, 16 ep   0.8092   <- the recipe BOTH leaderboard submissions used
  OneCycle,    no aug, 16 ep   0.8153   (+0.0061 from the schedule)
  OneCycle,    no aug, 40 ep   0.8181   best, but the tail DECLINES to 0.8043 by ep36
  OneCycle,    aug,    30 ep   0.8201   best, and the tail is FLAT (0.8172-0.8181 through ep29)

+0.0109 over the submitted recipe, and the overfitting is GONE rather than merely checkpointed around: the unaugmented 40-epoch run fell 0.014 from its peak, the augmented 30-epoch run falls 0.003.

That closes about half the 0.0236 per-member gap to their 0.8398, from two changes that were already written in our own code and simply not connected.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH KEEPING: epoch time fell 40s -> 30s from the memmap indexing fix (images[b, :, s:s+G] in one op rather than images[b][:, :, s:s+G], which materialised all twelve slices to use three). So the corrected recipe at 30 epochs costs about the same wall-clock as the old one at 16.
close_reason: fit_epoch now routes pixels through augment_bag; measured +0.0110 on fold 0, and a test asserts the CALLER not just the callee

title: Medial beats lateral on both pairs — is our laterality recovery wrong, or is it the labels?
description:
Per-label holdout AUC, our fold 0:

    Lateral Meniscus 0.742  vs  Medial Meniscus 0.785   (-0.043)
    Lateral OA       0.774  vs  Medial OA       0.840   (-0.066)
    MCL              0.747  vs  ACL             0.821

BOTH medial/lateral pairs favour medial, and the side-defined targets are exactly the ones a broken laterality normalisation would damage. That is a hypothesis, not a finding — medial pathology is also commoner and more often named in reports, which would produce the same asymmetry through label quality alone.

IT IS CHEAP TO SETTLE, and the audit found why: the diagnostic needs only HEADERS, not pixels. `Acquisition` already carries `laterality_tag` and `centre_x`, so resolving how each study's side was decided is ~24k header reads (~15 s with 20 workers). No cache rebuild.

MEASUREMENT: split the holdout three ways — side from the TAG, side from GEOMETRY, side UNRESOLVED — and compare the medial-minus-lateral AUC gap in each.
  - gap flat across all three  -> it is the labels; laterality is fine; this lead is dead.
  - gap worse on the geometry-resolved half -> our recovery is wrong, and it is worth more than any ensemble.
  - gap worse on the unresolved half -> those studies are being fed unmirrored and should be handled, not ignored.

The cache does NOT currently persist which rule decided each study, which is itself worth fixing once this is answered.
notes:
REFUTED (2026-08-11) — and cleanly, which is why it was worth running first.

PROVENANCE over 4407 studies (headers only, ~90s): tag 2203 (50.0%), geometry 2132 (48.4%), unresolved 72 (1.6%). On the 2135 studies where BOTH are available they agree on 98.6% (their notebook claimed ~97% for the same rule, so this validates the recovery on our corpus).

MEDIAL-MINUS-LATERAL AUC GAP, holdout of fold 0, split by how the side was decided:
  all (909)              meniscus +0.042   OA +0.060
  side from TAG (454)             +0.046      +0.036
  side from GEOMETRY (436)        +0.041      +0.085
  left knees, untouched (431)     +0.071      +0.074
  right knees, MIRRORED (459)     +0.015      +0.035

TWO REASONS THE HYPOTHESIS DIES:
1. Geometry-resolved studies show the SAME asymmetry as tag-resolved ones, so the recovery rule is not introducing it.
2. Decisively, the asymmetry is SMALLER on the knees we actually mirror (+0.015/+0.035) than on the ones we leave alone (+0.071/+0.074). A broken mirror would do the opposite.

So laterality is exonerated and the medial>lateral asymmetry is most likely prevalence/label driven: medial pathology is commoner and more often named in a report, so its derived labels are both denser and cleaner.

HONEST LIMIT: at ~450 studies per group these gaps carry roughly +/-0.02-0.03, so the tag-vs-geometry comparison is solid (it is the same number twice) while the left-vs-right split is suggestive rather than proven.

A METHOD BUG THIS FOUND, in the diagnostic itself: the first run computed the geometric side from only the UNTAGGED series of each study, which made 'both available' mean 'studies whose series disagree about having a tag' - a biased subsample of 74 that read as 86.5% agreement. Recomputing geometry from every series gave 2135 studies at 98.6%. The lesson generalises: when comparing two estimators, both must see the same input.
close_reason: Refuted: the asymmetry is identical across tag- and geometry-resolved studies and SMALLER on the mirrored knees. Laterality is exonerated; the cause is most likely label prevalence.

title: Overlap TTA at inference — implemented, free, and we submitted without it
description:
`Ensemble.predict_member` already takes `overlap: bool = False`, and both kernels call it without the argument. So both submissions averaged over 4 DISJOINT windows while their own inference path used 10 OVERLAPPING ones.

Costs one keyword argument and 2.5x a 0.3 s per-study step — against a 542 s fixed kernel cost, that is nothing. No retraining, no new decode: the cache already holds the slices.

Caveat worth measuring rather than assuming: the out-of-fold ablation found DISJOINT windows matched their stored predictions better (0.025) than overlapping (0.042). That was a statement about reproducing their OOF, not about which scores better. Run both against the same holdout locally before spending a submission.
notes:
MEASURED ON OUR OWN HOLDOUT (2026-08-11, fold 0, member_fold0):
  middle window only (1)   0.8092
  disjoint windows (4)     0.8180
  overlapping windows (10) 0.8205

So overlap is worth +0.0025 over disjoint and +0.0113 over a single window - free, no retraining, and the cache already holds the slices. Both submitted kernels used the DEFAULT overlap=False, so both left this on the table.

This also resolves the caveat: the out-of-fold ablation preferred DISJOINT because that reproduced THEIR stored predictions, which is a statement about matching their pipeline, not about which scores better. On our own holdout, overlapping wins. The two results do not conflict - they answer different questions.
close_reason: Measured (+0.0025) and enabled in both kernels: overlap=OVERLAP_TTA.

title: OneCycleLR: the plateau at epoch 12 is a missing schedule, not a missing epoch
description:
MEASURED: our five folds peak at epochs 13/13/10/12/11 and gain +0.0002/+0.0106/-0.0003/+0.0035/+0.0024 over their final five epochs. Training is saturated at ~12 epochs, so "they ran 60 epochs and we ran 16" does NOT explain the per-member gap (ours 0.8162, theirs 0.8398). Running longer at a constant learning rate would buy nothing.

AUDIT FOUND WHY: they wrap AdamW in

    torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=[LR_BACKBONE, LR_HEAD], total_steps=EPOCHS * (len(tr) // BATCH), pct_start=0.15)

We have no schedule at all — constant 1e-3 head / 8e-6 backbone. A constant LR that plateaus at epoch 12 while a one-cycle run keeps improving to 60 is exactly the shape you would expect, and it is the single most likely cause of the per-member gap.

PROVES IT: retrain fold 0 with OneCycle, same seed, same everything else. If the holdout peak moves past 0.8092 AND the peak epoch moves late, the schedule was the cause. If it plateaus at 12 again, the cause is elsewhere and this is closed.
notes:
CONFIRMED, then partly superseded (2026-08-11). Fold 0, matched — same seed, same data, only the schedule differing:

  constant LR,  16 epochs   0.8092  (peak ep13)
  OneCycleLR,   16 epochs   0.8153  (peak ep12)   +0.0061
  OneCycleLR,   40 epochs   0.8181  best, but the curve PEAKS near ep16 (0.8143) and then declines
                                     monotonically: 0.8118 / 0.8101 / 0.8071 / 0.8061 / 0.8043

So the schedule is a real +0.0061, and MORE EPOCHS IS NOT THE LEVER: past ~16-20 the model overfits. Their 60 epochs is not something to copy directly.

WHY THEY CAN TRAIN 60 EPOCHS AND WE CANNOT — see knee-<AUG>: our `augment` was never called. Every run to this point, including both submissions, trained with ZERO augmentation. The declining tail of the 40-epoch curve is what unregularised training looks like.

OFF-BY-ONE PAID FOR: total_steps used `len(training) // batch`, but our batcher KEEPS the final partial batch while theirs drops it. OneCycleLR raised on the last step of the whole run — after every epoch had been logged, before the checkpoint was written. Fixed with a ceiling rather than by discarding data.
close_reason: Confirmed +0.0061 and shipped; more epochs refuted as a lever (the 40-epoch tail declines without augmentation).

title: Leak-safe validation: split by report-text hash
description:
Some reports are byte-identical across studies (a template read for an unremarkable knee), so every study in such a group gets the SAME derived target vector. Splitting a group across the divide scores the model on a target whose source it trained on.

Assign studies by a hash of the report text so duplicate groups stay whole. Hold out one fifth, fixed rather than rotated.

TWO REFERENCES, TWO MEANINGS: the holdout measures agreement with derived targets and has the numbers to select epoch and recipe. The annotation check measures agreement with a radiologist - what the competition scores - but only annotated studies inside the holdout may be used, and there are too few, so it is REPORTED and never allowed to arbitrate. Annotated studies stay in training at elevated weight, which is exactly why the check must exclude them.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, train.csv, 4407 studies): 4276 distinct reports, so 177 studies sit in a duplicate group. Group sizes: 27 pairs, 10 triples, one of 4, four of 5, one of 6, one of 12, one of 14, one of 37.

The largest group (37 studies) is a Turkish all-normal template: 'Diz eklemi ici sivi miktari normal. Capraz ve yan baglar normal...'. Next are Spanish templates at 14 and 12.

So the leak is real but bounded - 4% of studies. Splitting by report hash costs nothing and removes it; the 37-group alone would otherwise straddle the divide.
EMPIRICAL SUPPORT FOR 'THE ANNOTATION CHECK MUST NOT ARBITRATE' (2026-08-10, from the 20 published members):

Members differing ONLY by fold and seed - same architecture, same data, same recipe - report annotation-check scores from 0.7356 to 0.9164. That is a 0.18 spread on a metric that is supposed to measure the same thing, and it matches the Hanley-McNeil prediction (SE ~0.09 at A~0.8 with single-digit positives) almost exactly.

Their holdout scores over the same 20 members span only 0.8279 to 0.8600 - a 0.03 spread, six times tighter.

There is also structure, not just noise: every fold-2 member has a HIGH holdout (0.857-0.860) and a LOW annot (0.736-0.795). The annotated studies are distributed unevenly across folds, so which fold a member held out changes what its annotation check even measures.

So: select on the holdout, report the annotation check, and never let a 0.18-wide instrument arbitrate a 0.01 decision.
close_reason: ReportFolds.assign hashes the REPORT TEXT so duplicate template reports never straddle the split; measured leak was 4 percent of studies. Split seed is separate from the model seed (--split-seed) after the bug where seed 7's fold-0 holdout shared only 192 of 909 studies with seed 2026's.

title: Slice ordering from geometry, never from file name
description:
Order each series by k = p.n where n = r_x cross r_y from ImageOrientationPatient and p = ImagePositionPatient. InstanceNumber is the fallback where geometry tags are missing (it tracks k up to sign, but interleaved/multi-echo acquisitions number out of spatial order and it is not signed in patient coordinates).

WHY: file names are SOP Instance UIDs - unique, not ordered. Sorting by them is reported at rho ~ 0.01 against physical position, and it fails SILENTLY: three-channel adjacent slices become three unrelated cross-sections, the middle of the stack becomes a random subset, and laterality reversal becomes a no-op.

PROVES: compute Spearman rho between filename order and geometric k on a sample of our series. Expect ~0.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, one 186-slice Philips series): Spearman rho(filename order, geometric k) = -0.0106. Filename order carries no anatomical information whatsoever.

Geometry tags are present on every slice of the sample: ImagePositionPatient 186/186, ImageOrientationPatient 186/186. So the exact ordering is available and the InstanceNumber fallback may be rarely needed - measure the tag-presence rate corpus-wide before relying on that.

k spans -68.6 .. 97.9 mm over the stack.
close_reason: acquisition.py orders slices by geometry via the through-plane projection k = p.(rx x ry), never by file name.

title: Series -> slot routing, with Fluid_Sensitive/Fat_Suppression recovered from the header
description:
Six slots: SAG_FLUID_FS, COR_FLUID_FS, AX_FLUID_FS, SAG_FLUID_NOFS, COR_T1, SAG_T1, plus a per-slot presence mask (a study rarely has all six).

MECHANISM: the shipped Fluid_Sensitive/Fat_Suppression columns are reported to agree on every training row, i.e. they carry ONE axis where the names claim two. Recover both from the header: weighting from TR/TE (T1: TR<~800; T2: TR>~800 and TE>~60; PD: TR>~800 and TE<~60), settled by ScanningSequence first because gradient echo breaks the TR rule; fat suppression from SeriesDescription/SequenceName/ScanOptions, falling back to TR/TE.

PROVES: on OUR copy of train_series.csv, measure the agreement rate between the two shipped columns. If it is 100%, the degeneracy is confirmed and recovery is mandatory, not optional.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, train_series.csv, 24371 rows): Fluid_Sensitive == Fat_Suppression on 1.000000 of rows. The crosstab is a clean diagonal - 10361 at (0,0), 14010 at (1,1), zero off-diagonal.

The two columns carry ONE axis, not two. Recovering both from the header (TR/TE/ScanningSequence for weighting, SeriesDescription/ScanOptions for fat-sat) is therefore mandatory, not an optimisation.

Corroborated by the sample series: SeriesDescription 'AX PD FS MPR L' with TR 1100 / TE 23 - TR>800 and TE<60 reads PD by the rule, and ScanOptions 'FS' gives the suppression independently. The rule reproduces the description.

Planes: Sagittal 9864, Coronal 8609, Axial 5898. Series per study mean 5.53, max 14 - so the six-slot scheme has real material to route.
IMPLEMENTED + MEASURED FROM THE PIXELS (2026-08-10). On 150 random series our recovered fat-suppression agrees with the shipped Fat_Suppression column on 99.3%, but our recovered fluid-sensitivity agrees with the shipped Fluid_Sensitive column on only 78.7%.

So the shipped pair is the FAT-SAT axis alone, wearing two names - the earlier finding that the two columns are identical on 1.000000 of rows said they carry one axis; this says WHICH one. The non-fat-suppressed pool is 40 T1 against 32 PD/T2, so routing on the shipped flags would put fluid-weighted series into the T1 slots for about a fifth of the corpus, and the presence mask would assert a sequence that was never acquired.

title: Graft: inference-only kernel from pilkwang's mounted weights -> LB floor
description:
Mount pilkwang/rsna-knee-weights + pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels + metaresearch/dinov2/PyTorch/small/1, run inference over the mounted test set, submit.

WHY: needs no local data and no training, and turns the field's public plateau (~0.899) into a measured number on OUR submission path. Same move as the biohub pilkwang graft.

HONESTY: the score is his result, not ours. Record it in comp/SUBMISSIONS.md as a graft; it must never appear in a README as our number, and it is a floor to build past, never an end state.
notes:
GRAFT, PHASE A IN PROGRESS (2026-08-10).

The weights manifest is fully self-describing: 20 members = 5 folds x 4 seeds, ALL one config (336px, 12 slices, group 3, crop 130mm, dinov2-small, cls_mean pool, prior false, unfreeze_last 6). One pixel_group, so a single decode serves all twenty. Their own numbers: holdout mean 0.8398 (min 0.8279, max 0.8600), annot mean 0.8375 (min 0.7356, max 0.9164).

Split into two phases because they have different prerequisites:

title: Sample more slices at inference than at training (the .903 recipe's 12 -> 32)
description:
The scored .903 EfficientNet-B3 reference samples 12 slices per series while TRAINING and 32 at INFERENCE. We use 12 for both, and our cache is built at 12 — but the cache only constrains TRAINING. The kernel decodes the test split fresh, so reading 32 slices there costs nothing but decode time and needs no retraining and no new members.

WHY IT SHOULD WORK, and it is not the same lever as TTA: overlapping windows (already measured at +0.0025) re-read the SAME twelve cached slices in different groupings. Thirty-two slices covers more of the joint — a Baker's cyst sits at the posteromedial end of a sagittal stack, and the band sampler at twelve slices may simply never sample it. More windows re-slices what we have; more slices sees what we did not.

COST: decode scales linearly, so ~1 s per study becomes ~2.7 s. Against a kernel whose fixed cost is 542 s and a hidden set of order a thousand studies, that is roughly 45 minutes — affordable, and the existing degradation ladder (fewer windows, then fewer members) already exists if a run runs long.

MEASUREMENT, which is CPU-bound and therefore parallel to any training: decode the fold-0 holdout at 32 slices into its own cache, then score the SAME member at 12 and at 32 and compare. If it helps, it is free at submission time; if it does not, the twelve-slice band is already covering what matters and that is worth knowing too.
notes:
REFUTED, with a mechanism (2026-08-11). Scored on fold 0's holdout with member_fold0, matched on everything but the slice count:

  12 slices, disjoint (4 windows)    0.8281
  12 slices, overlap (10 windows)    0.8316   <- best
  32 slices, disjoint (10 windows)   0.8140
  32 slices, overlap (30 windows)    0.8137

Reading MORE slices is 0.018 WORSE, and more windows over those slices does not rescue it (0.8140 vs 0.8137).

WHY IT DOES NOT TRANSFER, which is the useful part: our encoder input is THREE CONSECUTIVE SLICES STACKED AS CHANNELS. The band (0.20-0.80 of the stack) is fixed, so at 12 slices a 3-slice group spans a certain physical thickness, and at 32 slices the same group spans roughly a third of that. The model is then shown groups whose through-plane extent it never saw in training — a different input distribution, not merely more of the same one.

The .903 recipe can raise its slice count precisely because its pooling is MAX OVER SLICE EMBEDDINGS: each slice is encoded independently, so more slices is more samples of a distribution that does not change. Ours couples slice spacing to the input through the channel stacking.

SO THE IDEA IS NOT DEAD, IT IS CONDITIONAL: it becomes available only if the group's physical thickness is held fixed while the slice count rises (sample 32 positions but keep the 3-slice group spacing at the 12-slice pitch), or if the aggregation changes to per-slice encoding. Both are real experiments; neither is the free win the recipe made it look like.

CONFIRMS SEPARATELY: overlap beats disjoint again at 12 slices (0.8316 vs 0.8281, +0.0035), consistent with the +0.0025 measured earlier on a different member.
close_reason: Refuted at 12->32 for OUR architecture: 0.8137 against 0.8316. Channel-stacked slice groups couple spacing to the input distribution; conditional revival paths recorded.

title: Intensity augmentation from cardiac-seg: the axis the public baseline does not touch
description:
IDEA SOURCE: ../cardiac-seg/core/data/dynamic/augment.py, where gamma / contrast / blur / noise are the transforms that measurably closed a CROSS-VENDOR generalisation gap on cardiac MRI.

OUR AUGMENTATION IS GEOMETRY-ONLY, and so is the public baseline's: rotation 8 deg, scale 0.08, shift 0.05, and a single global gain 0.10. There is no gamma, no contrast, no blur, no noise anywhere in either.

WHY THIS CORPUS SHOULD CARE MORE, NOT LESS: reports arrive in nine languages, so the studies come from many countries and therefore many scanners and protocols. That is the same nuisance variance cardiac-seg was fighting, in a harder form — and the hidden test set is where it bites, which is exactly the axis a holdout on the same corpus flatters.

TRANSFERRED WIDTHS (cardiac-seg's, adjusted): gamma (0.7, 1.5) at p=0.3, blur at p=0.2, contrast (0.85, 1.15), noise 0.02 — noise cut from their 0.08 because theirs acts on z-scored images and ours on [0, 1].

WHAT DOES NOT TRANSFER, and why the reason matters more than the setting:
- FLIPS. They flip both axes freely; a cardiac label is not side-defined. Here a horizontal flip undoes the laterality normalisation five of the twelve targets depend on.
- TRANSLATION. They measured it NEUTRAL and turned it off because a fully-convolutional U-Net is translation-equivariant. Our encoder is a ViT with position embeddings and is NOT equivariant, so the same measurement should not be inherited — it has to be re-run here.

PROVES IT: fold 0, matched against the 0.8201 augmented-geometric baseline. Intensity augmentation should help the HIDDEN test more than the holdout, so a flat holdout with a better LB is a possible and interesting outcome — which is an argument for spending a submission on it rather than judging it locally alone.
notes:
ARM C — INTENSITY AUGMENTATION IS +0.0019 ON THE HOLDOUT (2026-08-11), which is small and honestly near the resolution of a single matched fold.

  baseline  geometric augmentation only          0.8202
  C         + gamma / blur / contrast / noise    0.8221   (+0.0019)

CONTEXT THAT KEEPS THIS HONEST: turning augmentation on AT ALL was worth +0.011 (the never-called bug). Adding the intensity block on top of that is worth about a fifth as much on this measurement.

THE PRE-REGISTERED CAVEAT APPLIES, and it was written before the result: this transform targets CROSS-SCANNER nuisance variance, and the holdout is drawn from the SAME corpus as training — same scanners, same protocols. A same-corpus holdout is close to blind to the thing intensity augmentation is for. The hidden test is where it would pay, and a flat holdout with a better leaderboard was explicitly listed as a possible outcome.

So the result is compatible with both 'it does very little' and 'it does something the holdout cannot see', and this measurement cannot separate them. What it does establish: it does not HURT, which is not nothing — an augmentation that widens the input distribution could easily have cost accuracy on the narrow distribution being scored.

DECISION: keep it available but do NOT enable it by default on the strength of +0.0019. It is worth one submission slot later, when a submission is being spent anyway, precisely because the leaderboard measures the axis the holdout cannot.
FULL 2x2 COMPLETE (2026-08-11), fold 0, every arm scored on the pilkwang ruler:

                      pilkwang labels   v4_blend labels
  geometric aug            0.8202           0.8194
  + intensity aug          0.8221           0.8203

  intensity augmentation:  +0.0019 (old labels), +0.0009 (v4)   -> mean +0.0014
  better labels:           -0.0008 (geom),       -0.0018 (intensity) -> mean -0.0013

BOTH IMPORTED IDEAS ARE NULL on this measurement, and there is no interaction to rescue either.

THE PATTERN THIS SESSION, stated plainly because it is the most useful thing learned:

  fixing OUR OWN broken code   augmentation never called  +0.0110
                               missing LR schedule        +0.0061
                               TTA default left off       +0.0035
                                                          -------
                                                          +0.0206

  importing ideas from         intensity augmentation     +0.0014
  research and notebooks       better label table         -0.0013
                               32 inference slices        -0.018
                               label fusion               -0.0016 (vs best single)
                                                          -------
                                                          net negative

Fixing what we had was worth an order of magnitude more than adopting what others had, and every imported idea needed adapting or died on a mechanism specific to our architecture. That is not an argument against reading the field — the READING is what found the schedule, and the .903 notebook is what made labels checkable at all — but it is an argument against assuming a published gain transfers.

WHAT REMAINS LIVE: member count, the one difference we KNOW separates our 0.868 from the 0.888 graft. Two extra seeds on fold 0 are training now to price a member.
CORRECTION (2026-08-11): closed as 'null' on a single-fold matched pair, but seed variance on the same fold is +/-0.012 while these effects are +/-0.002. The correct verdict is NOT DETECTABLE at n=1, not null. Neither is worth re-running bigger — resolving 0.002 against 0.012 needs ~36 paired runs — but the record should not claim more than it measured. See knee-uxg.

title: train.py holds the best checkpoint in memory until the very end
description:
`train.py` keeps `best_state` as an in-memory dict and only calls `torch.save` after the final epoch. A process that dies at epoch 29 of 30 loses the entire fold — about fifteen minutes at the current recipe, and considerably more if the resolution or epoch count grows.

It nearly cost us already: the OneCycle off-by-one raised on the LAST STEP of the whole run, after every epoch had been logged and immediately before the save. The run was a total loss despite having produced its best epoch twenty minutes earlier.

It also makes the machine's own documented weakness expensive: suspend/resume on this box has a track record of killing GPU-adjacent state (the vpcivsp/WSL wedge), so an interrupted long run is a realistic event rather than a hypothetical.

FIX: write the checkpoint whenever `best` improves, to a temp path renamed into place so a crash mid-write cannot leave a truncated file. Optionally record the epoch and the RNG state so a fold can resume rather than restart.

DO NOT APPLY MID-RUN: the five-fold loop invokes `python -m kneemri.train` fresh per fold, so editing the module changes the recipe for folds that have not started yet. Apply after the current run completes.
close_reason: Trainer.save_partial writes each new best atomically (temp+rename) rather than holding it to the end

title: Loss normalisation: we divide by total weight, they divide by element count
description:
Ours:   (BCE * w).sum() / w.sum().clamp(min=1)
Theirs: (BCE * w).mean()

With most weights below 1, dividing by the weight sum makes our gradients roughly twice theirs for the same batch, and it makes the effective step size depend on how confidently the batch happened to be labelled. Theirs is a fixed scale.

Our normalisation was chosen deliberately ("a batch carrying little confidence should not take a full-sized step on almost no evidence") and that argument is still reasonable — but it interacts with the missing schedule, and an effectively doubled LR that never decays is a good way to plateau early.

Test it as a PAIR with the schedule, not alone: schedule-only, then schedule + their normalisation, on fold 0.

title: Weight floor: a finding the report never mentions should pull weakly, not not at all
description:
We set the per-(study, target) loss weight to the confidence itself, so a target the report never mentions gets weight 0.0 and is DROPPED from the loss.

They use a floor:  W = 0.25 + 0.75 * conf  (annotated studies keep W = 3.0, which we already match).

The difference is not cosmetic. Silence in a radiology report is weak evidence of absence — a knee report lists what was checked and found intact, so an unmentioned finding is more often absent than present. Dropping it entirely throws that evidence away; a 0.25 floor keeps it at a quarter of the weight of an asserted one.

Pairs with knee-<LOSSNORM>: our loss divides by the total weight while theirs divides by the element count, so changing the weights also changes the effective step size. Change them together or neither, and measure both against fold 0.
notes:
RAISED IN PRIORITY by the augmentation find. Both the weight floor (0.25 + 0.75*conf vs our conf) and the loss normalisation (knee-sbr) are now the main un-tested differences from their recipe, since the schedule is measured (+0.0061) and epochs are refuted as a lever.

Test them against the AUGMENTED baseline, not the current one — the numbers below the augmentation fix are all from an unregularised model and are not the baseline anything should be compared to.

title: Treat the rare findings as the expensive ones
description:
Every label costs the same 1/12 of the score. A label left at chance contributes 0.5 instead of ~M, forfeiting (M-0.5)/12 however well the other eleven do - at M=0.85 that is 0.029, larger than most modelling gains.

So rare findings deserve MORE attention than common ones, because a rare finding is where a model most easily ends up at chance. Track per-label AUC from the first run and treat the worst label as the work item, not the mean.

Prevalence drift is survivable (AUC is in expectation invariant to positive rate, and the competition does not guarantee matched prevalence across train/public/final); thresholds are not.

title: Encoder adaptation: unfreeze the last blocks, two learning rates
description:
Adapt rather than freeze. Two restraints: only the last N transformer blocks move (early blocks are generic edge/texture filters - there may not be enough supervision to improve them and there is certainly enough to damage them), and the encoder learns far more slowly than the head (the head is random and has everything to learn; the encoder starts from a good solution and only needs moving off it). Reference point: head 1e-3 vs backbone 8e-6, last 6 blocks.

WHY NOT FROZEN: a frozen SSL encoder caps every downstream axis at once - resolution, size, coverage, aggregation all change how much it looks, none change the vocabulary it looks WITH. That ceiling should bind here: the features come from natural images, where nothing resembles a torn meniscus on a PD sequence.

title: Per-diagnosis query attention over slots, with a masked softmax
description:
Each of the twelve diagnoses gets its own query attending over the (up to six) slot embeddings, with absent slots masked OUT of the softmax so it renormalises over what the study actually contains.

WHY: mean-pooling the slots discards the reason the protocol has three planes - each finding is read on particular sequences, and a mean dilutes the one carrying the evidence with five that do not.

KEEP IT SMALL: the label is attached to the STUDY, so nothing in the supervision says which part carries the finding. Where the supervision is coarse, so is the head - a richer aggregator has no signal to learn from.
notes: IMPLEMENTED as kneemri/slot_head.py (SlotHead) during the Phase A port: per-diagnosis query, learned slot identity, masked softmax renormalising over present slots. Unit-tested including the property that masking a slot out equals never supplying it. Still to be trained by us - this is the replicated architecture, not our result.

title: Report-derived labels: adopt the public tables, then measure whether we can beat them
description:
Only a subset of training studies carry the twelve annotations; every training study carries a Report, and test.csv has NO Report column - so reports are training targets or sample weights, never an inference-time input.

Start by mounting the public LLM label tables (pilkwang, stevenleehans, lixin73-sol56) since every top notebook uses them. THEN attack them: labels are the ceiling on a weak-supervision task, and because the public tables are SHARED, improving them is edge nobody else has.

DIAGNOSTIC (needs no ground truth): the silence rate - for each (report, finding) pair, did anything match at all - tagged by language, says where the vocabulary is thin. Agreement-with-annotations cannot arbitrate: at A~0.8 with a handful of positives, the Hanley-McNeil SE is ~0.09, a 95% interval of +/-0.17, far wider than the differences being separated.
notes:
THE DEFINING FACT, measured (probe v2, train.csv 4407 x 14): all 4407 studies carry a Report, and only 58 carry all twelve annotations.

58 / 4407 = 1.3%. The competition is therefore a weak-supervision problem first and an imaging problem second: the labels for 98.7% of the training corpus have to be read out of free text, in nine languages, or not exist at all. This is why every top notebook mounts the same public LLM label tables, and why improving those tables is the highest-leverage un-shared axis available.

Prevalence among the 58 annotated studies: Effusion 0.603, Synovitis 0.466, Medial Meniscus 0.448, ACL 0.414, Lateral Meniscus 0.397, PF OA 0.362, Contusion 0.328, Fracture 0.310, Medial OA 0.259, Baker's 0.207, Lateral OA 0.190, MCL 0.155.

Read that as counts, not rates: MCL has NINE positives, Lateral OA eleven, Baker's twelve. Any model-selection decision made on the annotation check is being made on single-digit positive counts - which is exactly the Hanley-McNeil argument for why the holdout, not the annotation check, must arbitrate.
FIRST TRAINED MEMBERS (2026-08-10) on the public LLM report labels (pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels, CC0): 5 folds x 16 epochs, holdout mean AUC 0.8092 / 0.8177 / 0.8108 / 0.8179 / 0.8252, mean 0.8162. Selected on a holdout split by REPORT-TEXT HASH so duplicate reports cannot straddle the divide.

The published members average 0.8398 on their own holdout, so we are ~0.024 under the frontier after one training run. That gap is now a MEASURED quantity, which is what makes it attackable: the labels are the shared input everyone mounts, so beating the public tables is the un-shared axis - and our number moving without the labels changing would say the gap is in the model instead.

Training cost: 27s per epoch on the 5090 over the 35.8 GB memory-mapped cache. Cheap enough that epochs and folds are not the constraint - what to train ON is.
PRE-REGISTERED DECISION RULE for the next submission (2026-08-11, written BEFORE the folds finished):

SUBMIT if the new five-fold holdout mean is >= 0.825. Otherwise do not spend a slot.

Reasoning: the old ensemble averaged 0.8162 with a fold-to-fold spread of about +/-0.008, so anything under ~0.825 is inside that spread and proves nothing. Fold 0 has already reproduced +0.011 on a MATCHED comparison (same fold, same seed, only the recipe differing), and overlap TTA adds a measured +0.0025 on top, so the threshold is what the two changes should deliver if they hold across folds rather than being fold-0 luck.

Written down in advance so 'notable' cannot be decided after seeing the number.

title: Decode-once pixel cache under a memory budget
description:
Decode slot images once into a uint8 in-memory cache; bytes = studies * slots * slices * P^2. Training draws one group of consecutive slices per step (doubles as augmentation along the stack); inference averages over groups.

WHY: a study is ~150 files and the pipeline is read-bound, not arithmetic-bound. Affordable once, not once per epoch.

CONSTRAINT: the cache grows with the SQUARE of resolution and only linearly with slices, so slice coverage is the cheap axis and resolution the expensive one. Budget a fraction of free memory (not all of it) and size TRAIN + TEST caches together, since both are resident at once - overshooting ends the run rather than slowing it.

title: Physical-scale crop + resample (mm/pixel is the design variable)
description:
Crop to a constant physical extent L and resample to P pixels, so effective pitch = L/P mm/pixel.

MECHANISM: a feature of width d survives only if pitch <= d/2 (Nyquist on the resampling grid). A meniscal tear is 1-3mm, so 1mm needs <= 0.5 mm/px. At L=130mm: P=224 gives 0.580 (fails), P=336 gives 0.387 (clears). The crop must be SMALLER than the smallest field of view or it silently does nothing.

PROVES: measure the acquired FOV distribution (Rows * PixelSpacing) over our training series. The claim to check is median ~160mm, range 70-320, and that 130mm sits below the FOV of ~99.6% of series. Pick L from OUR measurement, not from the quoted one.

title: Laterality normalisation, including recovery when the tag is absent
description:
Five of twelve targets are side-defined (two menisci, medial/lateral OA, MCL). Normalise: flip the last axis for coronal/axial (medial-lateral is in-plane); REVERSE THE SLICE ORDER for sagittal (medial-lateral is the slice axis).

Laterality is Type 2C and reported absent on half the studies, by whole vendors. Recover from patient coordinates: image centre c = p + r*ds*Nc/2 + d*dr*Nr/2; +x points to the patient's left, so sign(c_x) gives the side. Use the CENTRE, not p (a corner half a FOV away can flip the sign near the midline). Leave a study unresolved inside a ~20mm dead band rather than guessing.

PROVES: on our data, measure the Laterality-tag absence rate and its per-vendor concentration; check the recovered side against the tag where both exist.

title: tests/e2e is still empty
description: The testing policy in CLAUDE.md specifies three layers; integration is now filled with the checkpoint-to-submission chain, e2e is still an empty directory. An e2e smoke would decode one REAL study from D:/data, build the cache, run a member and write a submission row - which is the only layer that would catch a DICOM-reading or slot-routing regression. It must skip when the data root is absent so CI stays green, which is also why it was not written blind: a test that always skips is worse than no test because it reads as coverage.
close_reason: tests/e2e/submission_smoke.py: four real studies through cache -> member -> prediction -> submission columns, plus a cache/model shape agreement check. Skips when the data root or a member is absent.

title: Queue scripts must use python -u and a real process-kill path
description: Two operational defects cost time this session. (1) Piping train stdout through grep buffers it, so a 45-minute arm showed NO epoch lines and progress could only be inferred from the .partial checkpoint mtime; python -u fixes it and is now used in the chain script. (2) pkill does not exist in this Git-bash environment - it fails with 'command not found' and the failure looks like success in a compound command, so an earlier 'kill the queue' silently did nothing. Use PowerShell Get-CimInstance Win32_Process + Stop-Process -Force, matching on CommandLine. Both are why a confounded arm ran for 7 minutes before being caught.

title: Non-English reports: weaker labels and a 0.016 score gap on 54% of the corpus
description: DEFLATED, do not build the parser on this evidence. The gap survives restricting to confident labels (0.0119 all vs 0.0117 at conf>=0.7), so it is not simply ruler noise. BUT scanner model predicts report language almost deterministically (MAGNETOM Avanto fit 0 percent english over 262 studies, Optima MR450w 100 percent), the between-manufacturer spread (0.8020-0.8256) is LARGER than the language gap and does not order by english share (best group is 50 percent english), and field strength shows nothing (1.5T 0.8159 vs 3.0T 0.8156). Language is confounded with site. Subgroups are small (111-223) so the manufacturer ranking is not itself established. A nine-language label parser targets the one reading the evidence does not isolate.

title: Two seed members on disk have an unrecoverable recipe
description: seed7_fold0.pt and seed13_fold0.pt were trained by an inline queue whose flags were not saved and whose script is gone. Checkpoints recorded image geometry but not one_cycle/weight_floor/intensity_aug, so neither can be matched to a seed-2026 counterpart and neither can serve as a noise floor on its own. train.py now writes an 'options' block (str-valued, since every loader uses weights_only=True and it refuses Paths). If a clean noise floor is needed, run three seeds under one explicit recipe rather than trusting these two.

title: Rebuild the kit whenever kneemri/ changes, not only when weights change
description:
A kernel run died on `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'kneemri.submission'`. The kernels had been refactored to import a newly extracted module, the MEMBERS dataset was pushed with the new weights, and the KIT — which is what actually carries our source into the kernel — was not.

`comp/verify_kit.py` exists precisely for this and takes a second to run. It was skipped because the change felt like it was 'only in the kernels', which is exactly backwards: the kernels are a bootstrap that imports the kit, so a change to either is a change to both.

CHEAP FIX AVAILABLE: make the push path refuse to run a kernel against a stale kit. `publish.py kernel` could call the same drift check `verify_kit.py` performs before pushing, so the ordering cannot be got wrong by remembering. Filed rather than done because the immediate cost was one kernel run and pushes are unlimited — but it will recur every time a module is extracted.
close_reason: publish.py now runs verify_kit's drift() in main, before auth, on every subcommand

title: cls_mean_focal pooling — implemented, unused by us AND by their shipped members
description:
`StudyModel._pool` already implements `cls_mean_focal`: class token, patch mean, plus the mean of the top eighth of each channel over the patch grid. Every published member uses plain `cls_mean`, so this is an untested axis for BOTH of us — an ablation, not a copy.

The rationale is quantitative: at 336 px the patch grid is 24x24 = 576 tokens, and a meniscal tear occupies a handful of them, so a plain mean dilutes the signal by roughly two orders of magnitude. That is the same argument the resolution choice was made on.

Costs one flag and a retrain (~5.5 min per member). Worth running against the settled recipe, not against the current one.

title: Scale to 20 members (5 folds x 4 seeds) — buys rank, teaches nothing
description:
The one difference we KNOW separates the two ensembles: theirs is 20 members (5 folds x 4 seeds), ours is 5. At ~12 epochs a member costs ~5.5 min, so 15 more is ~80 minutes, and members are nearly free at inference (20 members cost 575 s of kernel time against 5 members' 542 s — the fixed cost dominates).

Deliberately ranked BELOW the schedule and the diagnostic. It is the most predictable gain available and the least informative one: it would raise the leaderboard number while leaving every open question exactly where it is. Its real value is giving the other changes a stable ensemble to be measured against, so run it AFTER the recipe is settled, not before.
notes:
WHY THIS IS NOW THE PRIORITY, and how to measure it cheaply (2026-08-11).

The largest KNOWN difference between our 0.868 submission and the 0.888 graft is member count: 5 against 20. But the two also differ in per-member quality (0.8269 against their 0.8398), so the 0.020 leaderboard gap is a mixture of both and neither is attributable yet.

THE MEASUREMENT CANNOT BE TAKEN FROM WHAT WE HAVE. Our five members are five different FOLDS, so four of them trained on fold 0's holdout — ensembling them there would score a model on studies it was fitted on. Member count has to be varied with the fold held fixed, which means SEEDS.

QUEUED: two extra seeds for fold 0 (30 minutes), giving three members on one holdout. That yields the marginal-member curve — single member, then two, then three — and the shape of that curve says whether going to twenty is worth 2.5 hours of GPU or whether it saturates at four or five. Rank-averaging is the combiner, as the metric demands.

Ranked above further label work because arm A came back flat: the label lever is unproven on the model's own measurement, while the member lever is the one difference we KNOW separates our submission from the better-scoring one.
SEED VARIANCE IS +/-0.012, WHICH RETROSPECTIVELY WEAKENS MY OWN ABLATION CONCLUSIONS (2026-08-11).

Fold 0, identical recipe, identical data, only the seed differing:
  seed 2026   0.8202
  seed 7      0.8323     (+0.0121)

Every single-fold ablation I ran this session has an effect size FAR below that spread:
  intensity augmentation  +0.0019
  better labels           -0.0008
  both together           +0.0001

I reported those as 'null' and closed two issues on them. The honest statement is weaker: AT SEED 2026 the effects are small, and a single matched pair CANNOT RESOLVE an effect six times smaller than the run-to-run spread. 'Not detectable at n=1' is not the same as 'null', and I wrote the stronger claim.

WHY MATCHED SEEDS DID NOT SAVE IT, which is the subtle part: matching the seed fixes the initialisation and the data order, but every arm changes the random STREAM — augmentation draws differ, so the arms diverge stochastically much as different seeds would. Matched-seed is not paired in the way it looks.

WHAT SURVIVES: the five-fold result (+0.0107, every one of five folds improving) is a paired comparison across five independent splits, and five-for-five is not seed scatter. The bug fixes stand.

WHAT DOES NOT: the 2x2. To resolve a +0.002 effect against a +/-0.012 spread needs roughly (0.012/0.002)^2 ~ 36 paired runs, which at 15 minutes each is nine hours for one cell. That is not worth it for an effect that small — the correct conclusion is 'too small to matter at our current distance from the frontier', and the experiment should not be repeated bigger.

THE PROJECT'S OWN RULE SAID THIS: 'once a result works, multi-seed; never read signal into single-seed scatter'. I applied the first half and skipped the second.

SILVER LINING, and it is a real one: a +/-0.012 seed spread means ENSEMBLING SEEDS should pay well, because averaging independent runs of this variance is exactly what rank-averaging is for. That makes the member-count experiment more promising than it looked, not less.
VOID — THE MEASUREMENT WAS LEAKY, AND THE BUG WAS OURS (2026-08-11).

`train.py` built the fold split from the TRAINING seed: ReportFolds(folds, arguments.seed). So the extra seeds did not re-train the same setup on the same split — they trained on DIFFERENT splits. seed 7's fold-0 holdout shares 192 of 909 studies with seed 2026's.

CONSEQUENCES, all of them mine to retract:
1. 'Seed variance is +/-0.012' (0.8202 / 0.8323 / 0.8282) is unfounded — three numbers on three different holdouts of different difficulty, not three samples of one quantity.
2. The marginal-member curve (+0.0053 for the second member, +0.0018 for the third) is VOID: it scored seed 7 on seed 2026's holdout, 717 studies of which were seed 7's training data. That is what produced an implausible 0.8807 for a member that logged 0.8323 in its own run.
3. The correction I wrote to the interpretation document — downgrading the ablations against a +/-0.012 noise floor — rested on (1) and has itself been corrected.

THE BUG FAILED IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION, which is why it was worth catching: leakage makes numbers BETTER, so nothing looks wrong until a value is implausible enough to question. 0.8807 was implausible only because a matched measurement of the same member existed at 0.8316.

FIXED: --split-seed is now separate from --seed and defaults to 2026, so the split is a property of the corpus rather than of the run. A test asserts that changing the model seed does not move the split.

STILL UNMEASURED, and to be redone with the fix: the run-to-run noise floor, and the marginal value of a member. Both need seeds that differ ONLY in initialisation.
close_reason: Curve measured on the recovered ruler, three seeds, one split: 1 member 0.8204 [0.8171-0.8233], 2 members +0.0018, 3 members +0.0007. Best SINGLE member (0.8233) beats the 3-member ensemble (0.8229). Ensembling buys ~0.002 for 3x inference. Caveat: these differ only by seed on one fold, so it is a LOWER bound - the submitted 5-fold ensemble also varies training data.

title: comp/SUBMISSIONS.md: method-tuple naming + coverage grid
description:
Mirror the biohub convention: kernels named for the method tuple from a closed vocabulary, one subdir per method, and a coverage grid recording what has been tried vs what has not. The slug says which method it is; a new version of one slug is that same method retrained.

WHY: without it, submissions become an unlabelled pile and the 5/day budget gets spent re-running things whose result is already known. It is also where a grafted score is recorded AS a graft.

title: Decide whether to target the Efficiency Prize
description: Efficiency Prize: participation is automatic (905/905 teams ranked). Runtime weighted hard - the 0.940 model sits at efficiency rank 638. Teams at our exact 0.888 sit at ranks 29/33/50, so our accuracy run cheaply is a top-30 entry. BLOCKED ON knee-uxg: the decision is entirely 'what do members 2-5 buy', and that curve is currently void. Open risk: whether the board scores SELECTED submissions, in which case a fast entry competes with the accurate one.

title: Combine members by rank, not by probability
description:
The score is the unweighted mean of twelve per-label ROC AUCs, invariant under any strictly increasing map, so calibration and thresholds are worth exactly nothing.

Averaging raw probabilities lets the most confident model dominate; averaging RANKS combines the only information the metric reads. Applies to member ensembling and to TTA pooling (logit-averaging is a geometric mean of odds, probability-averaging an arithmetic mean of risk - they order studies differently).

title: Members carry their preprocessing; verify by fingerprint before use
description:
A trained member is only reproducible together with the reading that produced it: resolution, crop, slice-order rule, laterality rule, slot-fill predicate, and the stand-in for a slice that will not decode. NONE of those change a single tensor shape.

So a member fitted under one reading and run under another loads cleanly, runs, and returns a submission computed from the wrong image. Ship the reading WITH the member, and have each member answer a seeded question whose expected answer travels with it; a mismatch stops the run rather than being averaged into a submission.

Group members by the pixels they need so one decode serves every member sharing it.

title: Backbone ablation: DINOv2 vs medical-pretrained
description:
Every public notebook mounts metaresearch/dinov2/PyTorch/small/1. Alternatives are already packaged as Kaggle datasets: RadImageNet ResNet-50, MedicalNet ResNet-50 (3D), BiomedCLIP.

The field defaulted to DINOv2 with no visible evidence against domain-matched medical pretraining. Natural-image SSL may well win, but it is untested here, which makes this a cheap and uncrowded axis once a harness exists.

NOTE: no internet in kernels - a backbone must be a MOUNTED Kaggle model, never a download.

title: Graded targets + confidence as sample weights
description:
Reports are graded, annotations are thresholded: "small joint effusion" can sit against a NEGATIVE annotation because the annotator marked only significant ones. So "term present => positive" is wrong by construction; grade the mention (trace / unqualified / marked) instead - and it costs nothing, because the metric reads only order.

Carry a per-finding confidence as a sample weight so a report that never mentions synovitis pulls weakly on that head rather than asserting a negative. Weight the image-annotated studies above every derived row - they are the only labels read from the images.
